newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end flat to slightly higher Friday.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end flat to slightly higher Friday.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries prices ended flat to slightly higher in a shortened, pre-holiday session Friday that saw few participants actively trading.
The 30-year bond ended up 1/32 at 95-26/32 to yield 6.83 percent.

"There was not much going on this session. It seems nobody wants to believe any of the Fed commentaries or come to the realization they might raise rates," said Alan Levenson, money market economist at UBS Securities Inc. "They are going to wait for the data before making any moves."

Levenson said remarks made by outgoing Federal Reserve Board Governor Lawrence Lindsey were largely ignored as he will not vote at the next meeting of the policy-making Federal Open Market Committee on February 4 and 5.

"Trade and industrial production were stronger than expected, but the market held in anyway," Levenson said. The U.S. trade gap widened only 4.9 percent in November to $8.4 billion and industrial production rose 0.8 percent in December, above consensus expectations.
In addition, the University of Michigan preliminary January index showed consumer confidence slipped slightly to 96.0.
Levenson looked forward to Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan's testimony before the Senate Tuesday as the next market-moving event. The market is closed Monday for Martin Luther King Day.

"It's been pretty dull today. People are just kind of jerking around relative to their hedges versus corporates," said W. Michael McClure, head of government securities trading at Zions First National Bank.
McClure said that even though data released was negative, market participants were more concerned with selling some short positions and putting on new ones than in reacting to data.
He said the short end was seeing no selling pressure.
Chris Iggo, chief economist at BZW Securities Inc, said the early closing helped keep trading activity limited.

"There was good reaction to the Washington Post article (that called the likelihood of a tightening of monetary policy at the FOMC's February meeting small) and even though industrial production was strong, there was very little reaction to the data," said Iggo.

"The market wasn't terribly liquid and the strong dollar also helped bonds," he said. The dollar surged higher against the mark and yen Friday on the back of the strong industrial production and trade gap releases.

Two-year notes ended at 99-19/32, up 1/32, yielding 5.97 percent. Five-year notes were 3/32 higher to finish at 99-7/32, yielding 6.31 percent. Ten-year notes rose 2/32 to end at 99-20/32, yielding 6.55 percent.

Three-month bill rates fell one basis point and ended at 5.02 percent. Six-month bill rates were unchanged and finished at 5.07 percent. Year bill rates fell one basis point and ended at 5.29 percent.
